source: McClelland, McNaughton, O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems
finding: A back-propagation network trained on AB then AC lists loses the AB list almost completely before AC rises above 0 percent. Humans in the Barnes and Underwood data still recall over 50 percent after AC is learned.
numbers: Human AB recall above 50% at AC asymptote; network near 0% AB while AC still at 0% (McCloskey and Cohen 1989 simulation reproduced).
quote: complete abolition of AB list performance before AC rises above 0% correct
limits: This is a simulation of arbitrary paired associates, not of structured knowledge. French (1991) showed sparse codes cut overlap but also cut shared-structure use.
agent_relevance: Sequential fine-tuning on a new item can erase old items; the agent should not rely on one-pass updates to a shared store.

source: McClelland, McNaughton, O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems
finding: Core discriminating simulation: teaching Rumelhart's semantic network that penguins are birds that swim and cannot fly. Focused learning (new facts alone) learns fastest but damages other animals. Interleaved learning (new facts mixed with the full corpus) learns slower with almost no interference.
numbers: Same learning rate in both; interference measured as mean absolute error over the 15 'can' items in the base corpus; 100 presentations of penguin-can-swim-move-grow. Birds worsened most under focused learning; fish improved slightly.
quote: Interleaved learning allows the network to carve out a place for the penguin
limits: Neural-net simulation of one small domain; the new facts were inconsistent with old knowledge (this later proves to be the key boundary).
agent_relevance: Test every new lesson against a sample of old problems; do not accept a lesson that only fits new cases. Mixing old items into each update is the guard.

source: McClelland, McNaughton, O'Reilly (1995) Why there are complementary learning systems
finding: Reducing representational overlap avoids interference but costs the exploitation of shared structure (French 1991). The paper therefore argues for two systems rather than sparser codes in one.
numbers: Qualitative argument; cites Merzenich focal dystonia: repetitive focused practice reduced cortical differentiation, corrected by interleaved practice (personal communication, so not independently checkable).
limits: The Merzenich evidence is a personal communication, not a published study at the time.
agent_relevance: Keeping lessons sparse and separate (no overlap) avoids clashes but blocks generalisation; the schema should keep both a fast store of cases and a slow store of rules.

source: Kumaran, Hassabis, McClelland (2016) What learning systems do intelligent agents need? CLS updated
finding: Update of CLS. Hippocampus now also marks rare, salient events for preferential replay, so statistically unusual lessons are not swamped by typical ones. Replay may be interleaved with cortex-consistent activity rather than faithful old episodes.
numbers: No single number; theory review. Notes runaway repeated reactivation could explain PTSD.
quote: hippocampus ... marking salient but statistically infrequent experiences
limits: Review, not a test. Replay prioritisation is stated as mounting evidence, not proved.
agent_relevance: Replay selection should be weighted toward surprising or failed cases, not uniform.

source: Kumaran, Hassabis, McClelland (2016) What learning systems do intelligent agents need? CLS updated
finding: Challenge 1 to the 1995 theory: people infer across items never seen together (paired-associate inference, transitive inference) within one session, which looks like hippocampal generalisation. The REMERGE model explains this by recirculating several separate traces, and encoding-overlap models explain it by merged traces. Evidence does not yet discriminate them.
numbers: Sextet version tests A vs F links never co-presented; no effect sizes given in this review.
quote: empirical evidence to date does not definitely distinguish between them
limits: The review says both mechanisms may operate depending on paradigm, amount of training and delay. No clean winner.
agent_relevance: A fast case store may do some inference at read time (combining retrieved cases), so retrieval across stored lessons can generalise without slow rule learning.

source: Kumaran, Hassabis, McClelland (2016) What learning systems do intelligent agents need? CLS updated
finding: Challenge 2: with a prior schema, rats learn new flavour-place pairs in one trial and the memory survives hippocampal removal 2 days later (Tse et al. 2007). In a new arena no such fast learning occurs. A network trained on the animal domain learned schema-consistent facts fast without harming old knowledge and schema-inconsistent facts slowly.
numbers: Six PAs took multiple sessions over weeks; two new PAs learned from single exposure in the familiar arena; plasticity gene expression higher in neocortex 80 min after new PAs in familiar vs unfamiliar arena (Tse 2011).
quote: rapid systems-level consolidation ... is possible if the novel information is consistent with previously acquired knowledge
limits: The original 1995 simulations used schema-inconsistent items only, so this does not refute the interleaving claim for conflicting knowledge. Rat data, sample sizes not stated in the review.
agent_relevance: Boundary: lessons that fit the existing scheme can be merged at once; lessons that conflict need slow, interleaved checking against old cases. Route by consistency.

source: Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks (EWC)
finding: EWC slows learning on weights important to old tasks, framed as a synaptic-consolidation analogue. On Atari, plain SGD agents never learn more than one game and stay below a total human-normalised score of 1 out of a possible 10. EWC agents learn several games in sequence.
numbers: Ten Atari games, human-normalised score clipped to 1 per game, max 10; EWC did not reach the score of ten separate DQNs; true task labels gave only a modest gain over inferred labels. Permuted MNIST: more different tasks give more forgetting.
limits: Not an LLM. Fisher diagonal is an approximation; EWC stays below separate-network performance. Combined with DQN replay (two time scales).
agent_relevance: The authors themselves describe a two-timescale system (replay plus slow consolidation), the direct DQN-CLS link. Weight protection is not available to a scaffold-only agent; replay of cases is.

source: Rolnick et al. (2019) Experience Replay for Continual Learning (CLEAR)
finding: Mixing new experience and replay (50-50) with behavioural cloning almost removes forgetting in deep RL, close to separate or simultaneous training. 100 percent replay resists forgetting but slightly lowers peak score. 75-25 removes most but not all forgetting.
numbers: DMLab cyclic three-task sequence, final cumulative score, first task column: separate 29.24, simultaneous 32.35, sequential no CLEAR 17.99, CLEAR 50-50 31.40, no behavioural cloning 28.66 (table text garbled by extraction; column mapping inferred from row order).
limits: RL on DMLab and Atari, not language. Buffers of 5M vs 50M frames gave similar results.
agent_relevance: Interleaving ratio matters: a mix near half old, half new keeps both stability and plasticity. A rehearsal slice of old problems per lesson is cheap.

source: Chaudhry et al. (2019) On Tiny Episodic Memories in Continual Learning
finding: Training jointly on current data plus a tiny memory (even one example per class) beats purpose-built continual learning methods across four benchmarks. Repeatedly training on the tiny memory improves, not harms, generalisation.
numbers: Gains of 7 to 17 percent with one example per class; ER gain over FINETUNE and EWC about 15% at 1 example per class and about 28% at 13 per class; over A-GEM 1.7% (CIFAR, 1 per class) and over 5% (13 per class); reservoir sampling 3.5% worse than K-Means selection at one example per class.
limits: Single-epoch image classification. Reservoir sampling evicts early classes when memory is tiny, causing more forgetting.
agent_relevance: Which old cases you keep matters when memory is small: keep one per type (diversity-selected), not a random stream.

source: Arani, Sarfraz, Zonooz (2022) Learning Fast, Learning Slow: CLS-inspired general continual learning (CLS-ER)
finding: A direct CLS implementation: a working model, a fast plastic copy and a slow stable copy (two EMA averages) interacting with a small replay buffer, gives the best result on class-incremental benchmarks without task boundaries.
numbers: Text claims: in S-Tiny-ImageNet with buffer 200, CLS-ER gains 176% over ER and 114% over DER++; gap to DER++ grows with task difficulty and number of tasks. Table cells garbled in extraction, not quoted.
limits: Image classification; benchmark numbers from the authors' own runs; baselines from Buzzega et al. 2020.
agent_relevance: Two memory rates (fast cases, slow summary rules) outperform one; the scaffold could keep a fast lesson list and a slow vetted-rule list.

source: Kemker et al. (2018) Measuring Catastrophic Forgetting in Neural Networks
finding: A head-to-head test of five mechanisms (regularisation, ensembling, rehearsal, dual memory, sparse coding) on real images and audio finds that all fall well short of an offline model and the best mechanism depends on the paradigm. Rehearsal-type GeppNet did best at retaining the base set and learning new classes.
numbers: Metrics normalised by an ideal offline model, range 0 to 1; EWC, PathNet, GeppNet, GeppNet+STM, FEL compared; GeppNet+STM retained the base set well but failed to learn new sessions.
quote: the catastrophic forgetting problem has yet to be solved
limits: Older architectures and small tasks; authors state the problem has not been solved. Dual memory (STM) did not beat plain rehearsal here.
agent_relevance: Evidence that CLS-style dual memory is not automatically better than plain rehearsal: test the agent's memory against plain replay.

source: Luo et al. (2023) An empirical study of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during continual fine-tuning
finding: Forgetting appears in 1b to 7b models during continual instruction tuning and gets worse as scale rises within this range. Decoder-only BLOOMZ forgets less than encoder-decoder mT0. General instruction tuning first reduces later forgetting.
numbers: BLOOMZ at 1.1b, 1.7b, 3b, 7.1b; mT0 1.2b and 3.7b; domain, reasoning and reading tasks; forgetting measured as average decrease in retained score.
quote: as the model scale increases, the severity of forgetting intensifies
limits: Small scale range; authors suspect the scale trend reflects higher starting performance in the larger models. Not tested with replay.
agent_relevance: Bigger does not mean safer against forgetting; the lesson store must be checked regardless of model size.

source: Scialom et al. (2022) Fine-tuned language models are continual learners (CT0)
finding: Rehearsal of a tiny slice of old data lets T0 learn eight new generation tasks in sequence while keeping almost all earlier performance. At 0 percent rehearsal the model forgets T0 zero-shot tasks catastrophically. At 0.25 percent it is almost stable. At 1 percent it is stationary.
numbers: CT0 reaches 99.8% of the upper bound for T0pp and 98.0% for T0 3B after 8 tasks over 70 datasets; 1% replay buffer; result is task-order invariant (reverse-order run). LAMOL (generative replay) diverges from its upper bound.
quote: Continual Learning emerges from self-supervision pre-training
limits: Instruction-tuned seq2seq models; buffer is real data. Authors argue the stability comes from self-supervised pretraining. Generative pseudo-replay (LAMOL) did badly on these generative tasks.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct LLM evidence for the rule 'test new lessons against old problems': about 1 percent old data suffices. Real stored items beat model-generated ones in this study.

source: Ibrahim et al. (2024) Simple and Scalable Strategies to Continually Pre-train LLMs
finding: Learning-rate re-warming and re-decaying plus replay matches full retraining on all data, at 405M and 10B parameters. Replay fractions needed depend on shift size: 5 percent for a weak shift (Pile to SlimPajama) and 25 percent for a strong one (English to German).
numbers: 405M models with hundreds of billions of tokens; a 10B model also matched the retraining baseline; English evaluation averages within a range of 1.19 points (authors judge differences likely noise); more replay gave consistent gains when evaluating German-trained models on English.
quote: replaying previous data (as little as 1%) is sufficient to mitigate forgetting to a large extent
limits: Pretraining scale, not agent memory. German evaluations at 405M are near chance. Replay amount is shift-dependent, no universal ratio.
agent_relevance: Replay share should grow with how far the new lesson is from old ones; a fixed small share suits near-domain lessons only.

source: Biderman et al. (2024) LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
finding: Low-rank adapters learn less on the target domain but keep more of the base model on other tasks, a learning-forgetting trade-off. LoRA forgets less than weight decay or dropout, and forgetting grows with training length.
numbers: Code continued pretraining: best LoRA (rank 256) peaks at HumanEval 0.224 at 20B tokens, similar to full finetuning at 4B tokens (0.218); full finetuning peaks at 0.263. Instruction tuning max HumanEval 0.497 vs 0.263 for continued pretraining.
limits: Llama-2-7B, code and math only. LoRA and full finetuning lie on adjacent trade-off curves, with full finetuning preferable.
agent_relevance: Limiting how much a lesson can change the core (small, separable edits) lowers forgetting but also lowers learning; stability and plasticity trade off.

source: Kotha, Springer, Raghunathan (2024) Understanding catastrophic forgetting in LMs via implicit inference
finding: Fine-tuning appears to skew which task the model infers from the prompt rather than erasing ability. Conjugate prompting (e.g. translating the prompt) recovers lost capability: in-context learning lost through instruction tuning, reasoning lost after code tuning, and refusals bypassed after safety tuning.
numbers: Synthetic linear-function transformer setup plus real LLM tests; no single headline percentage in the abstract.
quote: fine-tuning skews this inference towards tasks in the fine-tuning distribution
limits: Hypothesis (implicit task inference) is supported mainly by a synthetic setup; recovery is partial.
agent_relevance: Forgetting may be partly a routing failure, so re-presenting old problems in a changed format is a diagnostic: if performance returns, the knowledge is not lost.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) Spurious Forgetting in Continual Learning of Language Models
finding: Large performance drops after new training often reflect lost task alignment rather than lost knowledge. Replay with 20 percent old data, regularisation, task vectors, gradient projection and generative replay all fail to prevent the first-steps damage. Freezing the bottom layers works best.
numbers: Old-task accuracy falls from near 100% to about 10% within the first 150 steps of new-task training; ten epochs on 10 harmful examples move LLaMa-2-7B-Chat safety from 0% back to about 99%; Freeze raises sequential fine-tuning accuracy from 11% to 44% while other methods peak at 22%; best gradient-projection variant 13.34%.
quote: performance drops ... reflect a decline in task alignment rather than knowledge loss
limits: Controlled synthetic dataset plus four real scenarios; theory rests on stated assumptions. Contradicts the idea that replay is enough in every case.
agent_relevance: Strong counter-result: replay at 20 percent did not rescue the alignment. A test that only checks old facts may miss lost task format; test old problems in their original format and a restated one.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Mitigating catastrophic forgetting in LLMs with Self-Synthesized Rehearsal (SSR)
finding: When old training data is unavailable, the model can generate its own rehearsal items by in-context learning from the base model, refine outputs with the latest model, and select diverse instances (1 or 10 percent). This keeps performance near rehearsal with real data.
numbers: SuperNI task sequences on Llama-2-7b and 7b-chat, ROUGE-L; random 1% selection shows small drops (roughly 0.2 to 2.9 points) in the reported tables; one k-means 10% row shows a much larger drop but the table layout makes the mapping uncertain, so not relied on.
limits: Table extraction partly garbled; synthetic rehearsal quality depends on the base model.
agent_relevance: If real old items are gone, self-written rehearsal is a fallback, but it inherits the model's own errors (G4), so it must be code-checked.

source: Gutierrez et al. (2024) HippoRAG: neurobiologically inspired long-term memory for LLMs
finding: A CLS-adjacent design: a knowledge graph plus personalised PageRank plays the hippocampal index and the LLM plays the neocortex. It integrates new knowledge by changing the index, not the model weights.
numbers: Up to 20 percent better than existing RAG on multi-hop QA; gains of about 3 and 20 points on MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA; single-step retrieval comparable to IRCoT while 10 to 30 times cheaper and 6 to 13 times faster; with IRCoT further gains up to 4 and 20 percent.
limits: Uses hippocampal indexing theory, not CLS interleaving; no forgetting test. First-author surname spelling from memory.
agent_relevance: A fast external index over stored lessons, with the slow model untouched, is the cheapest CLS analogue for a scaffold-only agent.

source: Lampinen et al. (2025) On the generalization of language models from in-context learning and finetuning
finding: With matched data, in-context learning generalises reversals and syllogisms more flexibly than fine-tuning. Fine-tuning on reversals embedded in a larger knowledge structure can generalise. Adding in-context reasoning traces to the fine-tuning data improves generalisation.
numbers: In the reversal-curse test, fine-tuning is near zero accuracy while in-context learning reaches ceiling (Fig 2); weaker but still visible ICL advantage on nonsense reversals.
limits: Synthetic datasets built to avoid pretraining overlap. A CLS author (McClelland) is on the paper but it runs no replay test.
agent_relevance: Fast in-context storage (a CLS fast learner) generalises better than slow weight updates for new facts: put new lessons in the prompt, not the weights.

source: McCloskey and Cohen (1989) Catastrophic interference in connectionist networks (as reported in McClelland et al. 1995)
finding: Original demonstration that sequential AB-AC training in a back-propagation network wipes the AB list, unlike the mild interference in human participants.
numbers: Numbers not read at source; the 1995 paper reproduces the curve (near-zero AB before AC rises).
limits: Not opened at source this session; used only via McClelland et al. 1995. The 1995 paper notes sparser codes can reduce the effect.
agent_relevance: Same as b01.

source: Tse et al. (2007) Schemas and memory consolidation (as described in Kumaran et al. 2016)
finding: Rats with a learned flavour-place schema consolidated new pairs in 48 hours, a hippocampal lesion after 48 hours spared the new memory, and no such effect occurred in a novel arena.
numbers: Exact trial counts and group sizes not read from source; the review gives six learned pairs and two new pairs.
limits: Not opened this session. Small rodent samples; replication status not checked here.
agent_relevance: See b06.

source: Tse et al. (2011) Schema-dependent gene activation and memory encoding in neocortex (as described in Kumaran et al. 2016)
finding: Follow-up: plasticity-related gene expression was greater in neocortex 80 minutes after new pairs in a familiar arena than in an unfamiliar one.
numbers: 80 minute time point from the review; counts not read at source.
limits: Not opened this session; same lab as the 2007 result, so this is an extension and not an independent replication.
agent_relevance: See b06.

source: Kumaran et al. (2016), DQN as a CLS-like system
finding: The review states that DQN-style replay of interleaved past episodes mirrors hippocampal replay into a slow learner, and that replay can be prioritised by reward and surprise as in the brain data.
numbers: No numbers; conceptual mapping.
limits: The map from experience buffer to hippocampus is an analogy, not a test.
agent_relevance: Prioritised replay is the AI counterpart; see the prioritised memory access subfield.

source: Rolnick et al. (2019), the 100 percent replay arm
finding: Training purely on replayed data still raises performance on each task even while on-policy learning is applied to another, but it lowers overall peak performance and slows early learning, notably on the hardest task.
numbers: Slight decrease in attained performance at 100% replay; most visible early on rooms_keys_doors_puzzle.
limits: Single RL setup; no variance reported in the text read.
agent_relevance: Never replay only old cases: new lessons need live exposure too. A 50-50 mix is the tested default.

source: Scialom et al. (2022), LAMOL versus rehearsal
finding: A generative-replay baseline (LAMOL, adapted to start from T0 3B) diverged from the upper bound, showing generated pseudo-samples were not enough on these generative tasks while 1 percent real rehearsal was.
numbers: Contrast with CT0 reaching 98.0 to 99.8% of upper bound.
limits: The authors hypothesise LAMOL suits NLU better than generation; one adaptation only.
agent_relevance: Prefer stored real cases over generated ones for old-problem tests.

source: Zheng et al. (2025), failure of replay and regularisation
finding: Storing 20 percent of old data and generating 24,000 pseudo old samples (LAMOL) both left the first-steps task-alignment drop in place; task-vector negation gave at best (95.76, 30.75) as old/new accuracy, or (99.41, 22.60) when new accuracy exceeded 99 percent.
numbers: Gradient directions that undo alignment have an average cosine similarity of only 0.4 across 10 trials.
limits: Synthetic task; damage is strongest early, so smaller or shorter updates may change the picture (not tested in the passage read).
agent_relevance: Damage happens in the first steps, so test after the first update, not only after training ends.
